sandhi.note: Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra.

morph.note: आह is a perfect form of the defective root √अह् ‘to say’, used with present or past sense; with प्र, प्राह ‘spoke out’. Here it announces the speech, and उवाच introduces it — a Purāṇic doubling of verbs of speaking.
Vocative of चामुण्डा, the name Kālī received for bringing Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa to the Goddess (7.27). The vocative of an ā-stem feminine ends in -e.
Past participle of वि + √स्तॄ (with -īrṇa): ‘spread out’. विस्तीर्णं वदनं कुरु, with a predicate accusative: ‘make (your) mouth wide’.

mantras.anvaya: तान् सुरान् विषण्णान् दृष्ट्वा सत्वरा चण्डिका प्राह; (सा) कालीम् उवाच — चामुण्डे, वदनं विस्तीर्णं कुरु।
mantras.lit: Seeing those gods dejected, Caṇḍikā spoke in haste; she said to Kālī: ‘Cāmuṇḍā, make your mouth wide.’
mantras.tr: Seeing the gods in despair, Caṇḍikā spoke at once. She said to Kālī: ‘Cāmuṇḍā, open your mouth wide.’

comm.t: Caṇḍikā answers the gods’ fear with a plan, and the plan is Kālī’s mouth. She addresses Kālī by the name she gave her in 7.27, Cāmuṇḍā.
The hymn of chapter 11 salutes this form as Cāmuṇḍā of the terrible tusked mouth (11.21 दंष्ट्राकरालवदने … चामुण्डे मुण्डमथने). The wide mouth commanded here is the image the hymn remembers.

flags.uncertain: प्राहसत्वरा is divided प्राह सत्वरा ‘spoke in haste’. The string could also be divided प्राहसत् ‘laughed aloud’ + त्वरा, but that would need the spelling प्राहसत्त्वरा and leaves त्वरा (nominative) without a construction; the reading itself is not in doubt.

samasa.literal: arisen from the fall of my weapons
samasa.sense: the blood my blows will draw from him

morph.note: Imperative of प्रति + √इष् (present stem इच्छ-): ‘accept, take in’. The same verb, with सम्, describes Cāmuṇḍā doing it in 8.59 (सम्प्रतीच्छति).
Ablative (= genitive) singular of the u-stem रक्तबिन्दु: ‘(born) from the blood-drop’, qualifying महासुरान्. See Uncertain.

mantras.anvaya: त्वम् अनेन वेगिना वक्त्रेण मच्छस्त्रपातसम्भूतान् रक्तबिन्दून् रक्तबिन्दोः (सम्भूतान्) महासुरान् (च) प्रतीच्छ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two objects of प्रतीच्छ: the blood-drops drawn by her weapons, and the asuras born of a drop.
mantras.lit: With this swift mouth of yours, catch the drops of blood that arise from the fall of my weapons, and the great asuras (that arise) from a drop of blood.
mantras.tr: With this swift mouth of yours catch the drops of blood my weapons draw from him, and the great asuras born from those drops.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Those drops’ generalises the singular रक्तबिन्दोः ‘from a drop’.

comm.t: Caṇḍikā’s plan has two parts: Kālī is to catch the blood before it reaches the ground (8.41 made the earth the condition), and to swallow any asura already born of it.

flags.uncertain: रक्तबिन्दोः (singular) is taken as ablative with महासुरान् (‘born from a drop of blood’). It could also be read as a genitive, ‘of Raktabindu’, as another name for Raktabīja; no other verse of the text uses that name, so the ablative is preferred.

morph.note: Simple future of √गम् with connecting i: गम्-इ-ष्यति. क्षयं गम् ‘go to destruction’ is a set phrase for ‘perish’.
Present participle, feminine, agreeing with the unexpressed ‘you’ of चर: ‘range (about), devouring’.

mantras.anvaya: रणे तदुत्पन्नान् महासुरान् भक्षयन्ती चर; एवम् एषः दैत्यः क्षीणरक्तः क्षयं गमिष्यति।
mantras.lit: Range in the battle devouring the great asuras born of it; in this way this Daitya, his blood wasted, will go to destruction.
mantras.tr: Range over the field and devour the great asuras born from his blood. So, drained of blood, this Daitya will perish.

comm.t: The plan’s logic: what cannot be killed by wounding can be killed by draining. Once no blood reaches the ground and none of the doubles survive, the source is exhausted.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa), in a separate work, names the Goddess महाकाली (751), महाग्रासा (752, ‘great devourer’) and महाशना (753, ‘great eater’). The devouring form commanded here is the kind of power such names describe; the two texts remain distinct.

sandhi.note: a + u → o twice (चोग्राः, चोत्पत्स्यन्ति); a + a → ā (चापरे); उग्राः loses its visarga before the voiced n.

morph.note: Passive present participle: the passive stem भक्ष्य- (with यक्) + मान: ‘being eaten’.
Future of उद् + √पद् (पद्-स्य → पत्स्य-). The root is ātmanepada and the classical form would be उत्पत्स्यन्ते; the parasmaipada ending is an epic (ārṣa) usage.
Absolutive of √वच् with samprasāraṇa (व → उ): उक्त्वा ‘having said’.

mantras.anvaya: त्वया च भक्ष्यमाणाः उग्राः (क्षयं यास्यन्ति), अपरे च न उत्पत्स्यन्ति च। इति तां उक्त्वा ततः देवी तं शूलेन अभिजघान।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends Caṇḍikā’s speech; its first clause leaves the verb to be supplied from 8.55 (‘will perish’). The second line is narrative.
mantras.lit: ‘And the fierce ones, being devoured by you, (will perish), and others will not arise.’ Having said this to her, the Goddess then struck him with the spear.
mantras.tr: ‘As you devour the fierce ones, no others will be born.’ So she spoke to Kālī, and then the Goddess struck him with her spear.
mantras.tr_note: The participial clause is rendered as a temporal clause (‘as you devour …’); the verb understood in the Sanskrit is left implicit.

comm.t: Caṇḍikā ends her instruction and acts at once: now that Kālī is ready to catch the blood, she herself wounds Raktabīja. शूल, translated ‘spear’ here, is also the word for the trident.

morph.note: Perfect of √ग्रह् in the ātmanepada: reduplicated ज-गृह्- with samprasāraṇa of र to ऋ. ‘She took (into her mouth)’.
Nominative masculine singular of the distal pronoun अदस् ‘that (one) yonder’. Before the vowel of आजघान its au becomes āv: असावाजघान.

mantras.anvaya: काली मुखेन रक्तबीजस्य शोणितं जगृहे; ततः अथ असौ तत्र चण्डिकां गदया आजघान।
mantras.lit: Kālī took Raktabīja’s blood with her mouth. Then he in turn struck Caṇḍikā there with his mace.
mantras.tr: Kālī caught Raktabīja’s blood in her mouth. Then he struck at Caṇḍikā there with his mace.

comm.t: The plan works at once: the blood from Caṇḍikā’s blow goes into Kālī’s mouth, not onto the ground. Raktabīja turns his mace on Caṇḍikā herself.
A modern reading: Caṇḍikā’s answer to an enemy who multiplies with every wound is not more wounding but removing the source. Kālī does not fight the doubles one by one; she stops them being born.
